note.question: How do quality and pricing decisions interact in a market with consumer information sharing?
note.overview: We provide a dynamic, game-theoretic model to examine a firm’s quality and pricing decisions for its new experience goods. Early consumers do not observe product quality prior to purchase but can learn it after purchase and share that product-quality information with later consumers—for example, through online reviews. Both the firm’s quality decision and its cost efficiency are the firm’s private information and not directly observed by the consumer.

source.quote: We provide a dynamic, game-theoretic model to examine a firm’s quality and pricing decisions for its new experience goods.
Early consumers do not observe product quality prior to purchase but can learn it after purchase and share that product-quality information with later consumers—for example, through online reviews.
Second, the ﬁrm chooses the quality level qi for its product.

After purchase, the ﬁrst-period customers learn the true quality and will share the information through product reviews or other forms of user-generated content, which we assume will reveal the true product quality to later consumers.
The ﬁrst-period consumers who bought the product will learn the true quality and reveal it to later consumers through user-generated content or word-of-mouth (either online or oﬄine).
Both the firm’s quality decision and its cost efficiency are the firm’s private information and not directly observed by the consumer.
The ﬁrm’s (constant) marginal cost is kq2, where q is the true product quality and k is a constant that represents the ﬁrm’s cost eﬃciency.
The consumer’s net utility from buying a product of known quality q
Without loss of generality, we assume k1 < k2—i.e., the type 1 ﬁrm is more cost eﬃcient than the type 2 ﬁrm and has a lower marginal cost for any given quality.

Note that in our setting, social learning (i.e., consumers’ information sharing) will fully reveal the ﬁrm’s quality and type in the second period; thus, reputation plays no role in our model, even though the ﬁrm’s second-period proﬁt depends on its earlier quality choice.
